# A year of remote work, and the part nobody warned us about

We closed the office in March. Nineteen people, one lease we let lapse, and a quiet confidence that the hard part would be tooling.

Tooling took eight days. Laptops, a VPN nobody liked, a Slack workspace that grew from four channels to sixty-one. Done.

The hard part was that meetings stopped being free. In the office, a decision cost somebody thirty seconds of walking. Remote, the same decision cost a calendar invite, and calendar invites are expensive, so people stopped asking and started guessing. Two teams shipped conflicting auth changes in June because neither wanted to book twenty minutes.

What fixed it wasn't more meetings. We wrote things down. Every non-trivial decision now goes in a plain markdown file in the repo: what we chose, what we rejected, who to argue with. It's ugly. It works. New hires read six months of context in an afternoon instead of pinging four people.

The second thing we got wrong: we assumed juniors would be fine. They weren't. Senior engineers thrived on the quiet. Juniors lost the overheard conversation, the shrug across a desk, the thirty small corrections a week that nobody schedules. We now pair two hours a day, on video, cameras optional. Our two most recent junior hires ramped faster than the ones we onboarded in the office.

Would we go back? No. But "remote is fine" was the wrong lesson. Remote is fine once you replace the things the building was doing for you without charging you for them.
